messages.subject: Identifying duplicate individuals
parts:
Dear Karl,

I followed the tutorial for genetic map construction to check if there were any individuals in my population with over 90% matching genotypes.  These pairs were identified as follows:

      row col
 [1,]  30  31
 [2,]  41  42
 [3,]  30  55
 [4,]  31  55
 [5,]  67  69
 [6,]  54  75
 [7,]  15  79
 [8,]  80  82
 [9,]  27  85

Next, I used a piece of code that I saw you suggest to another poster (since my organism has 20 chromosomes).  This removes 8 individuals from the analysis.  And the code I'm talking about is this:

for(j in chrnames(mapthis)) {
    g <- pull.geno(mapthis, chr=j)
    for(i in 1:nrow(wh)) {
        tozero <- !is.na(g[wh[i,1],]) & !is.na(g[wh[i,2],]) & g[wh[i,1],] != g[wh[i,2],]
        mapthis$geno[[j]]$data[wh[i,1], tozero] <- NA
    }
}

Now, my question:  I have not finished phenotyping all of my individuals.  Should I skip phenotyping the individuals that I know will get deleted due to them having more than 90% similar genomes?  If I wanted to do this, how would I identify which individuals these are?

The first "phenotype" column in my dataset is not a phenotype, but rather the number assigned to each individual.  For the pairs identified in the first part, does this refer to the individuals' order in my dataset?  Ie, for the pair (30, 31), does this correspond to the 30th and 31st rows in my dataset?

Hope this makes sense.

Thanks, 

Vanessa

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Identifying duplicate individuals
parts: Now, my question:  I have not finished phenotyping all of my individuals.  Should I skip phenotyping the individuals that I know will get deleted due to them having more than 90% similar genomes?  If I wanted to do this, how would I identify which individuals these are?
It depends on cost, and whether you'll have an opportunity to re-derive DNA and re-genotype the problem samples.

The first "phenotype" column in my dataset is not a phenotype, but rather the number assigned to each individual.  For the pairs identified in the first part, does this refer to the individuals' order in my dataset?  Ie, for the pair (30, 31), does this correspond to the 30th and 31st rows in my dataset?

Yes, those numbers are rows in the data. If you could include a phenotype column named "id", such identifiers will be shown instead.

karl
